name: Sleep to look attractive (beauty sleep research)

lead: Beauty sleep is the idea that enough sleep makes you look better. Appearance communities treat it as a baseline for a fresher, more attractive face, citing research in which sleep-deprived faces were rated as less healthy and less attractive.

Sleep medicine sources document visible signs of sleep loss, including eye bags, periorbital puffiness and styes, and in one study extreme sleepiness made people feel about 10 years older. Getting enough sleep avoids those signs. Studies that directly measured attractiveness ratings were not available to cite for this entry.

paras: People simply protect their sleep: regular bedtimes, a dark cool room and enough hours, usually seven to nine for adults. Visible changes around the eyes can show within days of sleeping better.

Sleep loss is linked to cognitive, mood and health effects. No risks of sleeping adequately are described. Persistent sleep problems despite adequate time in bed can reflect conditions worth discussing with a clinician.

angle.text: Enough sleep clears the visible signs of fatigue, such as puffy eyes, paler skin and droopy lids, so the face looks fresher and healthier. Studies have rated sleep-deprived faces as less healthy and less attractive.

lead: The idea of beauty sleep holds that adequate sleep improves how a person looks and that sleep-deprived faces are judged less attractive. It is a staple of appearance advice and looksmaxxing discussion.

Sleep medicine sources note that sleep deprivation produces visible signs including eye bags, periorbital puffiness and styes, and that extreme sleepiness made people feel about 10 years older in one study.[1] This article was written from limited sources; studies that directly measured attractiveness ratings were not available to cite.

paras: Reported visible effects of sleep deprivation include eye bags, puffiness around the eyes and styes.[1] Sleep loss is also associated with irritability and slower reactions, which affect presentation beyond the face.[1]
No studies found in the sources consulted for this entry on attractiveness ratings; the cited material covers general health effects of sleep deprivation only.[1]
